headline: Event-Driven Architecture: Decouple Systems at Scale
summary: Master the mental model behind event-driven systems. Learn how message queues decouple services, handle backpressure, and enable resilient scaling — without writing a single line of code.

slides.title: Your Microservices Are Tightly Coupled
slides.subtitle: Synchronous calls create brittle chains that cascade failures.
slides.body: When Service A calls Service B directly, a slowdown in B freezes A. One outage ripples through the entire system. How do you break this coupling?
slides.deep_dive: Modern distributed systems often default to REST or gRPC for inter-service communication. While simple, this creates temporal coupling — both services must be up, responsive, and correctly versioned simultaneously. A 500ms latency spike in a downstream service becomes a 500ms blockage upstream. Under load, thread pools exhaust, timeouts cascade, and the blast radius expands exponentially. Event-driven architecture inverts this: producers emit events and continue immediately; consumers process at their own pace. The queue absorbs bursts, retries handle transient failures, and services evolve independently.
slides.key_fact: Synchronous coupling turns partial degradation into total outage.
slides.why_it_matters: Decoupling via events is the single highest-leverage architectural shift for resilience.

slides.title: Think: Newspaper Subscription, Not Phone Call
slides.subtitle: Producers publish; consumers subscribe. No direct connection needed.
slides.body: A publisher drops a newspaper in a box. Subscribers pick it up whenever they're ready. The publisher doesn't wait. The subscriber isn't blocked.
slides.deep_dive: In a phone call (synchronous RPC), both parties must be available simultaneously. If one side is busy, the call fails or waits. In a newspaper model (event-driven), the publisher writes the story once and distributes it to a central location. Subscribers collect copies on their own schedule — morning, evening, or next week. The publisher never knows who reads it or when. The subscriber never knows who wrote it. This asymmetry is the superpower: new subscribers can join without touching publishers; publishers can scale without knowing consumer capacity. The message broker (the newsstand) handles storage, ordering, and delivery guarantees.
slides.key_fact: Events are facts about the past; commands are requests for the future.
slides.why_it_matters: This mental model shifts design from 'who do I call?' to 'what happened?'

slides.title: Input → Queue → Processing → Acknowledgment
slides.subtitle: The broker mediates; producers and consumers never touch.
slides.body: Producer sends event → Broker stores durably → Consumer pulls → Consumer processes → Consumer acks → Broker removes.
slides.deep_dive: The execution path has five distinct stages. First, the producer serializes an event (JSON, Avro, Protobuf) and sends it to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Pulsar, SQS). The broker appends it to a partitioned log or queue, replicating across nodes for durability — this is the 'commit' moment. The producer receives acknowledgment and continues; latency is typically sub-millisecond. Consumers, running independently, poll the broker for new events. They deserialize, execute business logic (send email, update search index, trigger workflow), then send an acknowledgment. Only after ack does the broker advance the consumer's offset or delete the message. If processing fails, no ack is sent — the broker redelivers after a visibility timeout, enabling at-least-once semantics.
slides.key_fact: The broker is the contract; schema registry enforces compatibility.
slides.why_it_matters: Durability + acknowledgment = exactly-once processing is achievable.
slides.input: Domain event: { orderId, customerId, amount, timestamp }
slides.processing: Broker partitions by key; consumers scale horizontally per partition
slides.output: Downstream effects: inventory reserved, email queued, analytics updated

slides.title: Gain Resilience, Accept Complexity
slides.subtitle: Event-driven isn't free — understand what you trade.
slides.body: You gain: decoupling, elasticity, replayability. You pay: eventual consistency, debugging difficulty, operational overhead.
slides.deep_dive: The trade-off table is stark. Synchronous calls give you immediate consistency — you know the result before returning. Event-driven gives you eventual consistency — the effect happens 'soon.' This breaks mental models: 'I placed an order but inventory hasn't reserved yet.' Debugging shifts from stack traces to distributed traces across async boundaries. You need correlation IDs, structured logging, and observability tooling. Operationally, you now run a message broker — a stateful, distributed system requiring monitoring, capacity planning, and upgrade strategies. But the payoff: consumers can crash and restart without losing events; new consumers can replay history; traffic spikes absorb into the queue instead of crashing services. Latency becomes predictable (queue depth) rather than cascading.
slides.key_fact: Eventual consistency is a feature, not a bug — it enables availability.
slides.why_it_matters: Choose event-driven when independence matters more than immediacy.

slides.title: Don't Treat Events Like RPC Responses
slides.subtitle: ❌ Waiting for consumer result defeats the purpose.
slides.body: Antipattern: Producer publishes event, then polls for consumer response. This re-couples services and adds latency.
slides.deep_dive: The most common regression is sneaking request-response semantics back into event-driven systems. A team publishes 'OrderCreated' then immediately queries a 'OrderStatus' API waiting for 'InventoryReserved.' This defeats decoupling: the producer now depends on consumer latency and availability. If the consumer is slow, the producer blocks. If the consumer crashes, the producer times out. The correct pattern: publish and forget. The producer returns 'OrderAccepted' to the user immediately. The consumer processes asynchronously. The user sees 'Order Confirmed' via websocket, polling, or email when processing completes. This requires UX changes — but those UX changes are the price of true decoupling. Another antipattern: fat events with entire domain objects. Events should be minimal — just the fact and a reference. Consumers fetch details if needed.
slides.key_fact: If you wait for a response, you built RPC with extra steps.
slides.why_it_matters: Async UX (notifications, polling) unlocks the architecture's value.

slides.title: How Netflix Handles 1B+ Events/Day
slides.subtitle: Event-driven is how planet-scale systems stay up.
slides.body: Netflix uses Kafka as the nervous system. Services emit lifecycle events; hundreds of consumers process independently for recommendations, billing, analytics.
slides.deep_dive: At Netflix scale, synchronous calls would create a mesh of death. Instead, every service publishes domain events to Kafka topics — 'MemberSignedUp', 'TitlePlayed', 'RatingSubmitted'. These events flow through a multi-region Kafka deployment with mirroring. Downstream, dozens of consumer groups process independently: the recommendation engine updates ML features in real-time; the billing service aggregates usage; the content team tracks popularity; security audits anomalies. Each consumer scales horizontally by adding partitions. When a new feature needs historical data, they replay from the beginning — no schema migration, no coordination. During the 'Squid Game' launch, traffic spiked 100x. Producers kept accepting writes; queues absorbed the burst; consumers scaled out automatically. No cascading failures. The broker is the shock absorber.
slides.key_fact: The queue is the circuit breaker for the entire architecture.
slides.why_it_matters: Event-driven turns traffic spikes into queue depth — a solvable ops problem.

slides.title: When to Go Event-Driven
slides.subtitle: Apply this pattern when coupling pain exceeds complexity cost.
slides.body: Use events for: cross-service workflows, audit trails, async UX, polyglot teams. Avoid for: simple CRUD, low-latency reads, small teams.
slides.deep_dive: The decision framework: if two services must deploy together, share a database, or call each other synchronously — that's coupling debt. Event-driven pays it down. Start with one boundary: the noisiest synchronous call. Introduce a broker. Publish a slim event. Build one consumer. Measure: did deployments decouple? Did latency variance drop? Did incident blast radius shrink? If yes, expand. If the team spends more time debugging distributed traces than shipping features, pause. Invest in observability first. Schema registry (Confluent, Apicurio) is non-negotiable — enforce backward/forward compatibility. Dead-letter queues with alerting catch poison pills. Idempotency keys on every event enable safe retries. And always design the UX for async: 'Your request is processing' beats a spinning wheel that times out.
slides.key_fact: Start with the most painful synchronous boundary — not the whole system.
slides.why_it_matters: Incremental adoption beats big-bang rewrites every time.
takeaways: Decouple deployments with events; accept eventual consistency
Slim events + schema registry + idempotent consumers = production ready
Design UX for async (notifications, polling) — don't fake sync over async

slides.title: Your 30-Day Event-Driven Sprint
slides.subtitle: Pick one boundary. Ship one event. Measure the difference.
slides.body: Week 1: Identify the tightest coupling. Week 2: Add broker + publish slim event. Week 3: Build idempotent consumer. Week 4: Add DLQ, monitoring, schema registry.
slides.deep_dive: Don't boil the ocean. Find the service call that causes the most incidents — the one where a downstream outage takes you down. That's your candidate. Set up a managed Kafka (Confluent Cloud, AWS MSK, Redpanda) or RabbitMQ. Define one Avro/Protobuf schema for the event — just the aggregate ID, event type, timestamp, and correlation ID. Publish from the producer; return 202 Accepted immediately. Build a consumer that processes idempotently (use the event ID as deduplication key). Add a dead-letter queue with PagerDuty alert. Instrument: publish latency, consumer lag, processing duration, error rate. After 30 days, compare: deployment frequency, incident count, mean time to recovery. The numbers will tell you if the complexity was worth it. Spoiler: for any non-trivial system, it usually is.
slides.key_fact: Managed brokers remove operational excuses — start there.
slides.why_it_matters: Proof beats debate. Ship a slice, measure, decide.
takeaways: Target the highest-coupling service boundary first
Use managed broker + schema registry from day one
Measure deployment independence and incident blast radius
